strengths: The paper addresses an important efficiency problem: reducing the visual prefix processed by a large language model. Combining class-attention outlier selection with key-based token merging is a simple, potentially useful adaptation of token reduction to multimodal models.

The reported compression is substantial: approximately 40 retained tokens instead of 576. Evaluation covers six benchmarks and both 7B and 13B LLaVA-1.5 models. After fine-tuning, ScienceQA and POPE performance remains close to, or slightly exceeds, the original models.

The ablations provide useful evidence for individual components. In Table 3, training-free PruMerge achieves 54.00 on TextVQA versus at most 47.96 for spatial sampling. Table 4 shows that token supplementation improves MME from 1221.6 to 1350.3 over selection alone.

The high-level pipeline and visualizations are understandable. The manuscript acknowledges prior pruning and merging methods, attributes its models and datasets, and explicitly discusses lossy compression and limited validation scope.
weaknesses: The central practical efficiency claim is insufficiently validated. Table 2 reports roofline estimates for LLM prefill under one assumed prompt length, rather than measured runtime and memory. It does not establish end-to-end gains after accounting for vision encoding, selection and merging overhead, decoding, or batching variable-length visual prefixes.

The comparisons do not establish the advantage of the distinctive algorithmic choices. Table 3 primarily compares against retaining the first 40 tokens and uniform spatial sampling. Matched-budget attention top-k selection and an adaptation of the cited token-merging method are missing. Table 4 supports supplementation but does not isolate the benefit of IQR-based adaptivity. Accuracy-versus-token-budget curves would substantially strengthen the contribution.

The accuracy losses are more substantial than the repeated claims of comparable performance and preserved reasoning suggest. In Table 1, 7B VQAv2 falls from 78.5 to 72.0 and MME from 1510.7 to 1350.3; 13B VQAv2 falls from 80.0 to 72.8. These may be worthwhile tradeoffs at this compression level, but they require more calibrated claims. Table 5 also shows that training-free POPE drops from 85.9 to 76.2, with recovery depending on additional fine-tuning.

Important implementation details are missing or inconsistent. The manuscript does not specify the neighbor count k or attention-head aggregation. Algorithm 1 excludes the selected center from the neighbor search and replaces it with an unnormalized weighted sum, whereas the prose describes supplementing retained tokens through weighted averaging. This affects the actual representation passed to the projector. LoRA hyperparameters are also omitted, and code availability is only promised.

Generalization evidence is narrow: both tested model sizes share the LLaVA-1.5 architecture and 336-pixel input resolution. High-resolution images and videos motivate the work but are not evaluated. The claim that adaptive token counts track image complexity is supported mainly by selected visualizations, without aggregate token-count statistics or a controlled comparison against fixed budgets.
